chapter: Bob Lyons band and New Orleans musicians
title: Bob Lyons, his crooked band and its members
summary: He describes bandleader Bob Lyons as crooked with money, lists sidemen (Bonnie Pigar, Charlie Decanje, Bill Matthews) and a big trombonist who lost both legs.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: No, get him to tell more about Bob.

He said he wants you to talk some more about Bob Lyons. Oh, Bob Lyons? Yeah. Yeah, Bob he said, plenty of kid bands, you know. And, but he was like that crooked. He was like that crooked. Yeah. Yeah. Bob was taking money on the job, you know. And then when we go on the job, you know, we had to come short all the time. Bob didn't get deposit and do spending. And then he said, I'm going to pay you on the next job. Well, then I did. I said, all of us left him, you know. We stayed with him about six or seven months. He was crooked all right. Yeah, yeah.
Who did they have with him?

Who did they have with him then? What he had with him? Yeah. You might know the fellas. I was playing with him at the time. Bonnie, Bonnie Pigar, yeah, him. And his brother, drum, yeah. We were playing together. Alex. Yeah. And then Charlie, Charlie Decanje, he was blowing trumpets. He's up there. Real light fella. Yeah, he's up there, but he don't play. He's a policeman up there now. Where? Where's the policeman at? I believe in Chicago. And, uh, what's the other fella named? Bill Matthews, he was playing drums. Yeah. You know him, eh? Oh, he remember the worst thing. He beat me. Yeah, he's a trombone player now, yeah. He was playing with athletes. But the team now, you know, after he got a new outfit. Oh, Bill Matthews is a lucky fella. Bill Matthews is a lucky fella. Bill Matthews is a lucky fella. Yeah. Yeah. Bill Matthews is a lucky fella. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He got a wonderful break. Yeah. Well, who played trombone with Bob Lyons? Who played trombone with Bob Lyons? Big Ernie Skelly. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

You know, it was very big, about six feet and so many inches tall, you know. And we had to get all beautiful and put them all in together, you know. So, and I got, me and Ernest went together, you know. And when I met with Ernest's house, Ernest's pants could make me a whole suit. I asked, I said, what make I have to pay the same thing Ernest paid? Ernest take up all that good. He said, well, we have to go through the same thing we do with you, we do with Ernest. I couldn't understand it, you know. He kept six too, he had diabetes, he cut one of his legs off. He went blind, then his eyesight came back, then he cut his other leg off. And after that, he died, you know. He wasn't here when he died, eh? No. He was a good trombone player too.
